items.item: the Raft leader coordinates all writes to its group and heartbeats followers, who become candidates and hold new elections if heartbeats stop

A majority quorum's safety guarantee doesn't come from any one majority being large — it comes from the fact that any two majorities drawn from the same group must overlap by at least one member, so two different majorities can never commit conflicting values without that overlapping member having agreed to both.

Refusing a write below quorum isn't a conservative default that could be relaxed for availability — accepting a write without quorum would let two disconnected minorities both believe they're authoritative, which is the exact split-brain scenario consensus exists to prevent.

etcd's own single-replication-group design is a deliberate trade, not an oversight: the documentation itself states it buys a simpler protocol and lower latency specifically because the whole dataset is small enough that one group suffices — it isn't the right choice at a scale where that assumption breaks.

at.step: Reveal: one global group vs. many per-range groups

items.item: Per-range consensus multiplies the number of leader elections and heartbeat streams a cluster has to run, proportional to the number of ranges — the blast-radius improvement this topic measures isn't free; it's a real operational cost traded for a smaller failure domain.

A cross-range transaction's extra round trips come from needing agreement at two separate levels at once: each range's own consensus group must agree internally, and then the ranges themselves must agree with each other that both sides are ready to commit — two-phase commit coordinates the second level, not the first.

Multi-Paxos, as DynamoDB documents using it per partition, solves the identical per-partition quorum problem Raft solves in CockroachDB and TiKV — the algorithmic difference between Paxos and Raft (left to Chapter 14) doesn't change this topic's own operational claims about blast radius or round-trip cost.

Kafka's KRaft quorum is deliberately small (typically three or five controllers) and separate from the much larger set of brokers it coordinates — the controllers alone need quorum; a broker going down doesn't touch the metadata quorum at all.

This topic's own 'Prove it' answer generalizes the per-range result directly: a failure that removes exactly one member from several independent groups is a fundamentally different event from one that removes a majority from a single group, even when the total number of affected members is identical.

This topic's own executable claims use a fixed, named set of unreachable members rather than a randomized failure model, specifically so the majority-vs-unanimity and global-vs-per-range contrasts are deterministic and don't depend on which particular members happen to fail in a given run.

The theory of how Raft and Paxos themselves reach agreement (leader election, log replication, the Paxos protocol's own phases) is assumed from Chapter 14 rather than re-derived here — this topic's own contribution is entirely about where that theory runs operationally and what it costs.
